cards.title: 6.1 Simple and Compound Interest
body: 6.1 Simple and Compound Interest

**Definition:** **Simple Interest** is a financial charge calculated strictly on the original principal amount borrowed or invested, represented by the formula $$I = Prt$$. **Compound Interest** is interest calculated on both the original principal and the accumulated interest from previous periods, represented by the formula $$A = P(1 + r/n)^{nt}$$.

### Deep Dive
Interest is the fundamental mechanism of the global banking system, serving as the cost of borrowing capital or the reward for lending it. When capital is borrowed, lenders charge a fee for the opportunity cost of losing access to those funds and the risk associated with lending. Conversely, when an individual deposits money into a savings account, they are effectively lending their funds to the bank, which uses that capital to issue loans and pays the depositor a portion of the returns as

cards.title: Business Mathematics
body: In compound interest models, the growth of capital is exponential. At the end of each compounding period, the interest earned is added to the principal, forming a new, larger base for the next period's interest calculation. This compounding effect means that the capital grows at an accelerating rate over time. This non-linear growth is the primary driver of wealth accumulation in retirement accounts and long-term investments, often referred to as the "time value of money."

cards.title: Business Mathematics
body: To analyze these models over time, we can use exponential equations. For example, if you want to find how long it will take an investment of $$5000\text{ Nakfa}$$ to grow to $$20,000\text{ Nakfa}$$ at a $$5.2\%$$ annual interest rate compounded annually, you must solve the exponential equation $$20,000 = 5000(1.052)^t$$. Using logarithms, this simplifies to $$t = \frac{\log 4}{\log 1.052} \approx 27.4\text{ years}$$. This shows how logarithmic functions are essential for solving practical financial problems.

cards.title: Business Mathematics
body:
| Parameter | Simple Interest Model | Compound Interest Model |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Growth Profile** | Linear (constant growth rate) | Exponential (accelerating growth rate) |
| **Calculation Base**| Original Principal ($$P$$) only | Principal ($$P$$) + accumulated interest |
| **Governing Formula**| $$A = P(1 + rt)$$ | $$A = P\left(1 + \frac{r}{n}\right)^{nt}$$ |
| **Primary Use Cases** | Short-term loans, basic treasury bills | Savings accounts, mortgages, retirement funds |

> **💡 Did You Know?**: Compound interest is so powerful over long periods that if a single Nakfa had been invested at a 5% interest rate compounding annually in the year 0 CE, its value today would exceed the total material wealth of the entire planet!

cards.title: 6.2 Installment Plans and Annuities
body: 6.2 Installment Plans and Annuities

**Definition:** An **Installment Plan** is a commercial purchasing agreement where the buyer takes immediate possession of an item by paying a down payment, and agrees to pay off the remaining balance plus interest through a series of regular periodic payments.

### Deep Dive
Installment plans are a common feature of modern consumer economies. They allow buyers to purchase expensive items, such as appliances, vehicles, and real estate, without having to pay the entire purchase price upfront. In a standard installment agreement, the purchase is broken down into a **down payment** (or deposit) paid at the time of purchase, and a series of **regular monthly payments** (or installments) that cover the remaining balance and finance charges.

body: interest.

In simple interest models, the growth of the capital is linear. The interest earned or charged during each period is constant because it is calculated only on the initial principal ($$P$$). For example, if you invest $$3500\text{ Nakfa}$$ at a $$5\%$$ simple interest rate per year for $$3\text{ years}$$, the interest earned each year is a flat $$175\text{ Nakfa}$$, resulting in a total interest of $$525\text{ Nakfa}$$ ($$I = 3500 \times 0.05 \times 3$$). This model is easy to compute but does not reflect the compounding behavior of modern financial accounts.

cards.title: Business Mathematics
body: The frequency of compounding ($$n$$) is a key parameter in compound interest calculations. Interest can be compounded annually ($$n=1$$), semi-annually ($$n=2$$), quarterly ($$n=4$$), monthly ($$n=12$$), or even daily ($$n=365$$). As the compounding frequency increases, the accumulated amount $$A$$ also increases, though at a decreasing rate. Calculating these values for large exponents is made easier by using logarithms and scientific calculators.

cards.title: Business Mathematics
body: Understanding the mathematical difference between simple and compound interest is critical for making informed personal finance decisions. When borrowing money, such as for a car loan or credit card, consumers should look for simple interest or low compounding frequencies to minimize their borrowing costs. Conversely, when saving or investing, they should seek accounts with high compounding frequencies to maximize their long-term returns.
